name: Lut (Lot)
source: Stories of the Prophets — compiled from the Qur'an and authentic hadith
paras: "And Lut believed in him. Abraham said: 'I will emigrate for the sake of my Lord. Indeed He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.'" (Al-'Ankabut 29:26). Lut was the nephew of Ibrahim; he believed in Allah alongside his uncle and migrated with him from Ur toward the land of Canaan.

While Ibrahim settled in Canaan, Lut was guided to the valley of Sodom, where he was sent as a prophet to its people. The land was green and watered, but its people had fallen into a sin no nation before them had committed — approaching men with desire instead of women, alongside robbery and evil in their gatherings.

Lut called them with patience for years: "Will you not fear Allah? I am a trustworthy messenger to you, so fear Allah and obey me. I do not ask you for any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds." (Ash-Shu'ara 26:161-164).

His people answered only with mockery: "Bring us the punishment of Allah, if you are of the truthful." They threatened to expel him and his family from the city, complaining that Lut and his followers kept themselves too pure.

The angels came to Lut in the form of handsome young men — the same angels who had first visited Ibrahim with the news of a son and of the coming punishment. Lut, not knowing who they were, was distressed: his people were the most corrupt of creatures, and he could not protect these guests.

The people came rushing at night to his house, demanding his guests. Lut said, "These are my guests, so do not disgrace me" (Al-Hijr 15:68). They pressed on, and Lut, powerless, said: "Would that I had power against you or could take refuge in a strong support." (Hud 11:80).

Then the guests revealed themselves: "O Lut, we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you." (Hud 11:81) — and Ibrahim's earlier plea for the people of Lut was answered: the decree had come, and it would not be turned back.

The command was given: "So travel with your family during a portion of the night and let not any of you look back — except your wife; indeed she will be struck by that which strikes them. Indeed their appointment is the morning. Is not the morning near?" (Hud 11:81).

When the decree arrived at sunrise, Allah turned the cities upside down: "So We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon them stones of layered hard clay." (Al-Hijr 15:74). The Dead Sea shore remains a sign: "Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers." (Ash-Shu'ara 26:174).

Lut's wife, who sympathized with the sinners and betrayed her husband's mission, was among the destroyed — Allah sets her forth as an example for the disbelievers (At-Tahrim 66:10). Lut himself was saved, honoured by Allah as a prophet and a righteous servant.
The lesson of Sodom is eternal: when a society legalizes what Allah has forbidden and mocks every warning, its destruction is only a matter of the appointed morning — "Is not the morning near?"
